summary: Discusses differences between IS-IS as used to route IP traffic in RFC 1195 and the way it is deployed today, to help implementers, testers and operators. A companion document, RFC 3719, covers the ISO 10589 side. It is informational.

plainLanguage.summary: IS-IS (Intermediate System to Intermediate System) is the protocol a network's own routers use to work out the best path to each destination. This memo lists the points where the IS-IS written down in RFC 1195 and the IS-IS that runs in real networks have drifted apart, so that people who build, test and run it know which reading to follow.

subtitle: Where the IS-IS written down in 1990 and the IS-IS that runs in the field have drifted apart.

tldr.problem: IS-IS was written down for IP networks in 1990, and several of its original design choices have since been changed in practice, so people building and running it had no single description of what the protocol now does.
tldr.mechanism: The memo goes through the protocol feature by feature and records what RFC 1195 says beside what deployed routers actually do: unused TLVs, the Overload Bit, narrow and wide metrics, hello packets, the attached bit, default routes, mixed protocol networks and interface addressing.
tldr.outcome: It is an Informational memo, so it specifies no standard and changes nothing in the protocol. It points at RFC 3719 for the same question asked about the ISO 10589 side of the protocol.

facts.label: Where the Overload Bit is set

today: RFC 3787 is an Informational memo published in May 2004, and it has not been obsoleted or updated. It describes the state of IS-IS practice at the time it was written: the differences between RFC 1195 and deployed routers, and the steps for moving a network from narrow metrics to wide ones.

sections.title: What This Document Is For
sections.content:
Interior Gateway Protocols such as IS-IS are designed to give timely information about the best routes in a routing domain. The original design of IS-IS, as described in ISO 10589, has proved to be quite durable, but a number of the original design choices have been modified in practice.

RFC 3787 lists the differences between the protocol as described in RFC 1195, which is the version of IS-IS written for IP and dual environments, and the protocol that can be observed on the wire today. The memo says it is offered as a service to those implementing, testing and deploying IS-IS to route IP traffic. A companion document, RFC 3719, covers the same ground for the ISO 10589 side of the protocol.

The document is an Informational memo. It says so in its status line: it provides information for the Internet community and does not specify an Internet standard of any kind. The key words MUST, MUST NOT, SHOULD, SHOULD NOT and MAY in it carry the meaning given in RFC 2119.
sections.plainLanguage: IS-IS lets the routers inside one network tell each other the best path to each destination. This memo is a list of the places where the written-down protocol and the protocol that actually runs have drifted apart.

sections.title: Features That Are No Longer Used
sections.content:
Two features defined in RFC 1195 are not in current use.

The first is the Inter-Domain Routing Protocol Information TLV, code 131, which was designed to convey information transparently between boundary routers. TLV 131 is not used, and an implementation MUST ignore it if it is received.

The second is the Authentication TLV, code 133, which carried information used to authenticate the PDU. This TLV has been replaced by TLV 10, described in RFC 3567, IS-IS Cryptographic Authentication. TLV 133 is not used either, and MUST be ignored.
sections.plainLanguage: Two pieces of the original IS-IS specification are never used. A router that receives either one is told to ignore it, so old software on one side of a link does not upset a new router on the other.

sections.title: The Overload Bit
sections.content:
To deal with transient problems that stop an IS from storing all the LSPs it receives, ISO 10589 defines the LSP Database Overload condition in section 7.3.19. When an IS is in that condition it sets a flag called the Overload Bit in the non-pseudonode LSP number Zero that it generates. Section 7.2.8.1 of ISO 10589 instructs other systems not to use the overloaded IS as a transit router. The overloaded IS does not have complete information, so it may not be able to compute the right routes, and routing loops could develop. An overloaded router may still be used to reach End Systems directly attached to it, because it may provide the only path to one.

The meaning of the flag has since been used for something else as well. In a service provider's network, when a router running both BGP and IS-IS reboots, BGP might take longer to converge than IS-IS. The router may drop traffic for destinations it has not yet learned through BGP, and it is convenient to set the Overload Bit until BGP has converged, as described in RFC 3277. An implementation SHOULD use the Overload Bit to signal that it is not ready to accept transit traffic.

An implementation SHOULD NOT set the Overload Bit in PseudoNode LSPs that it generates, and Overload bits seen in PseudoNode LSPs SHOULD be ignored. RFC 1195 makes clear in section C.1.4, which describes the SPF algorithm for IP routers, that directly connected IP subnetworks are reachable when an IS is overloaded. So when a router processes LSPs received from a router that has the Overload bit set in LSP number Zero, the receiving router SHOULD treat all the IP reachability advertisements as directly connected and use them in its SPF computation. Because the IP prefixes that an overloaded router announces are treated as directly attached, an overloaded router SHOULD take care in selecting which routes to advertise in the LSPs it generates.
sections.plainLanguage: The Overload Bit is a flag a router sets in its own link-state packet to say that other routers should not send traffic through it to somewhere else. Its database is incomplete, so the shortest paths it works out can be wrong, and a wrong path can send traffic in a circle. The addresses it advertises are still treated as directly attached, so the machines hanging off that router stay reachable.

sections.title: Moving from Narrow Metrics to Wide Metrics
sections.content:
IS-IS measures the cost of a link so that routers can compare paths. The IS-Neighbors TLV (TLV 2) defined in ISO 10589 and the IP Reachability TLV (TLV 128 and TLV 130) defined in RFC 1195 provide a 6 bit metric for the default link metric to the listed neighbour. This metric proved too limited. The Extended IS-Neighbors TLV (TLV 22) and the Extended IP Reachability TLV (TLV 135), defined in RFC 3784, give a 24 bit metric and a 32 bit metric for IP networks and hosts.

If not all devices in the IS-IS domain support wide metrics, narrow metrics MUST continue to be used. Once every device in the network can support the new TLVs, the network can be migrated to the new metric style, though care must be taken to avoid routing loops. The memo makes three assumptions about the implementation: each system can generate and understand both narrow and wide metrics; the implementation can run the SPF algorithm on an LSP database that holds instances of both metric styles; and if there are two metric styles for a link or IP prefix, one of them is picked as the true cost for that link.

To compare the variants of the narrow metric with wide metrics, the narrow metrics have to be mapped into a common integer range. The default metric is read as a 7 bit quantity: metrics with the external bit set are in the range [64..127], and metrics with the external bit clear are in the range [0..63]. The Most Significant Bit on an L1 metric tells whether the route has been leaked down, but it does not change the distance, so it is ignored.

The transition itself runs in five steps, taken in order. First, all routers advertise narrow metrics as defined in ISO 10589 and consider narrow metrics only in their SPF computation. Second, each system is configured in turn to send wide metrics as well as narrow metrics, and the two metrics for the same link or IP prefix SHOULD agree. Third, when all systems are advertising wide metrics, each system makes any changes necessary to consider wide metrics during the SPF, and changes MaxPathMetric to 0xFE000000. Fourth, each system is configured in turn to stop advertising narrow metrics. Fifth, when the network is only using wide metrics, metrics on individual links may be rescaled to take advantage of the larger metric.

That algorithm assumes the two metrics are equal. Section 5.2 covers the case where they are not: the SPF picks the minimum metric for each link, which may give a path with some links chosen because of a wide metric and some because of a narrow metric. The variables MaxPathMetric and MaxLinkMetric SHOULD retain the values defined in Table 2 of section 8 of ISO 10589.
sections.plainLanguage: IS-IS gives every link a cost, and routers compare paths by adding up costs. The original cost number had 6 bits, which was too small for big networks. The memo gives a five-step plan for moving every router to the wider numbers without breaking the paths: advertise both, use both, drop the old ones, then rescale.

sections.title: How IS-IS Routers Fit Together
sections.content:
The original intent of RFC 1195 was to provide a routing protocol capable of handling both CLNS and IPv4 reachability information. To allow CLNS end stations to know that they are attached to a router, intermediate systems are required to send Intermediate System Hello PDUs for end stations when a point-to-point circuit comes up. An IS is also not allowed to send IS-IS Hello PDUs (IIH) before it has received an ISH from a peer, which reduces routing protocol traffic on links with a single IS. In an IP-only environment the original need for the ISH PDU is not present. An IP-only implementation SHOULD issue an ISH PDU as described in section 8.2.3 of ISO 10589, to inter-operate with implementations which require an ISH to initiate the formation of an IS-IS adjacency. An IP-only implementation may issue an IIH PDU when a point-to-point circuit transitions into the Up state to initiate the formation of an adjacency, without sending an ISH PDU, but that may not inter-operate with implementations which require an ISH. An IS may issue an IIH PDU in response to the receipt of an IIH PDU in accordance with section 8.2.5.2 of ISO 10589, even though it has not received an ISH PDU.

ISO 10589 section 7.2.9.2 gives an algorithm for deciding when the attachedFlag should be set on an intermediate system. Some implementations also allow the attachedFlag to be set on ISs routing IP traffic when there is a default route in the local routing table, or when some other state is reached that implies a connection to the rest of the network.

RFC 1195 states in section 1.3 that default routes are permitted only at level 2 as external routes, included in the IP External Reachability Information field, and are not permitted at level 1. Because of the utility of the default route when dealing with other routing protocols, and because of the ability to influence the exit point from an area, an implementation MAY generate default routes in Level 1.

RFC 1195 assumes that every deployment of IS-IS routers supports a homogeneous set of protocols. It anticipates OSI only, IP only, or dual OSI and IP routers, and it allows only IP traffic in mixed areas, so it provides only lowest common denominator routing. It also requires the inclusion of the Protocol Supported TLV, code 129, in IIH and ISH PDUs and in LSP number Zero. IP capable routers MUST generate that TLV and MUST include the IP protocol as a supported protocol. A router that does not include it may be assumed to be a pure OSI router, and can be interpreted as implicitly advertising support for the OSI protocol. The behaviour of mixed networks that do not follow these guidelines is not well defined. The ITU-T requires that SONET/SDH equipment running IS-IS must not form an adjacency with a neighbour unless they share at least one network layer protocol in common, and a definition of an interoperable strategy for resolving the problems in non-homogeneous protocol networks remains incomplete.

On adjacency creation, RFC 1195 says that adjacencies are formed without regard to IP interface addressing, but many current implementations refuse adjacencies based on interface addresses and related issues. Section 4.2 of RFC 1195 requires routers with IP interface addresses to advertise those addresses in an IP Interface Address TLV (132) carried in IIH PDUs, and some implementations will not interoperate with a neighbour router that does not include it. Some implementations will not form an adjacency on broadcast interfaces with a peer who does not share an interface address in some common IP subnetwork. In a LAN that mixes implementations, care must therefore be taken when assigning IP addresses: if not all routers on a LAN are on the same IP subnet, DIS election may fail, leading to the election of multiple DISs on a LAN or to no DIS at all. Even if DIS election succeeds, black holes can result, because the IS-IS LAN transitivity requirements of section 6.7.3 of ISO 10589 are not met. Unnumbered point-to-point links do not have IP interface addresses, though they may have other IP addresses assigned to the routers, and the addresses on an unnumbered link do not need to be related. To interoperate in a mixed environment, an implementation MUST include an IP Interface Address TLV (132) in its IIH PDUs, and the network administrator should ensure that there is a common IP subnet assigned to links with numbered interfaces.
sections.plainLanguage: Routers become neighbours by exchanging hello packets. The rule for starting that exchange was written for a different protocol, and the memo tells IP-only routers what to do instead. It also warns that routers have to advertise their own interface addresses, or some of them will refuse to become neighbours at all.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content: The clarifications in this document do not raise any new security concerns, as there is no change in the underlying protocol described in ISO 10589 and RFC 1195. The memo notes one thing for people auditing a network: the document makes clear that TLV 133 has been deprecated and replaced with TLV 10.
sections.plainLanguage: The memo adds no new security risk, because it changes nothing in the protocol itself. It does record that the old authentication TLV has been replaced by a different one.

viz.caption: THE TLV CODES THIS MEMO MENTIONS

items.label: IS-Neighbors TLV
items.desc: Carries the default link metric to the listed neighbour, in 6 bits.

items.label: Authentication TLV
items.desc: The replacement for TLV 133, defined in RFC 3567.

items.label: Extended IS-Neighbors TLV
items.desc: Carries a 24 bit metric, defined in RFC 3784.

items.label: IP Reachability TLV
items.desc: Carries a 6 bit metric for IP networks and hosts. TLV 130 is the second form.

items.label: Protocol Supported TLV
items.desc: Must appear in IIH and ISH PDUs and in LSP number Zero. IP routers must list the IP protocol.

items.label: Inter-Domain Routing Protocol Information TLV
items.desc: Not used, and must be ignored if received.

items.label: IP Interface Address TLV
items.desc: Carries the router's IP interface addresses in IIH PDUs.

items.label: Authentication TLV
items.desc: Not used, and must be ignored. Replaced by TLV 10.

items.label: Extended IP Reachability TLV
items.desc: Carries a 32 bit metric for IP networks and hosts, defined in RFC 3784.
